1. In a cohort, S(t) just before month 12 is 0.80. At month 12, 70 members are at risk and 3 drop out. What is S(12)? Is the hazard in that month 3/70 or 3/100 of the original cohort, and why?

S(12) = 0.80 × (1 − 3/70) = 0.80 × 67/70 = 0.80 × 0.957 = 0.766. The month’s hazard is estimated as 3/70 = 0.043 per member-month, because only the 70 still enrolled and under observation could drop out that month. Members who had already dropped out or been censored are no longer in the at-risk set, so dividing by the original 100 would understate the rate.

2. In a two-year follow-up of TB patients, the Kaplan–Meier curve ends at 0.64. A colleague reports “median survival 24 months”. What should be reported instead?

The curve never falls to 0.5, so the median is not reached. Report “median NR” and give survival at stated times, e.g. “64% surviving at 24 months” (with its CI). Twenty-four months is simply the end of follow-up, not a median.

3. Why is a member who moves away at month 5 not simply deleted from a Kaplan–Meier analysis, and what assumption makes it safe to treat them as censored?

They were known to be enrolled and event-free for 5 months, and that is real information: they count in the at-risk set, in every denominator, up to month 5. Deleting them would discard it and bias the sample towards those with complete follow-up. Treating them as censored is valid under non-informative censoring: households lost to follow-up are assumed as likely to drop out later as similar households that remained under observation. (If moving away itself ended membership, it would be a competing event, §14.8.)

1. A Kaplan–Meier curve for Group A lies above Group B’s throughout follow-up, and the log-rank test gives p = 0.03. A colleague concludes: “Group A has a lower hazard at every single time point, guaranteed.” What is the overreach?

Two overreaches. First, S(t) is cumulative: a curve that stays higher reflects the sum of all hazard up to t. Group A can have a higher hazard than Group B during some periods and still keep a higher S(t), because of an advantage built up earlier; hazards can cross while survival curves do not. Second, the log-rank test is an overall test across the whole follow-up. p = 0.03 is evidence that the survival experiences differ overall, not a guarantee of anything at each time point, and nothing in statistics is “guaranteed”.

2. A two-group log-rank analysis gives O = 30, E = 24 in Group A and O = 20, E = 26 in Group B. Compute Σ(O − E)²/E, its df and approximate p-value.

χ² = (30 − 24)²/24 + (20 − 26)²/26 = 36/24 + 36/26 = 1.500 + 1.385 = 2.88, df = 2 − 1 = 1. The 5% critical value for 1 df is 3.84, so p > 0.05; exactly, p ≈ 0.09. No convincing evidence that survival differs, though Group A had 6 more events than expected.

3. Why can the log-rank test not tell you whether the intervention’s association with dropout remains after adjusting for household income?

The log-rank test compares groups defined by one categorical variable. It has no way to include a continuous covariate such as income, and it gives no effect size. Cox regression (§14.6) includes several predictors at once and gives an adjusted hazard ratio with a CI.

1. A Cox model reports HR = 0.6 for a treatment, but the two groups’ log(−log S) curves clearly diverge over log time, and the Schoenfeld residual test gives p = 0.002 for treatment. What does this mean for the single HR of 0.6?

Proportional hazards is violated: the treatment’s hazard ratio changes over follow-up. HR = 0.6 is a weighted average of different effects at different times (for example, strong early and weak later) and should not be read as applying throughout. Report time-specific HRs (split follow-up into periods), let the treatment’s effect vary with time (a treatment × time interaction), or, if treatment is only a covariate to be controlled for, stratify on it (§14.6.3 shows how).

2. A Cox coefficient is b = −0.35 with SE 0.12. Give the HR and its 95% CI, and state the result in hazard language.

HR = e^(−0.35) = 0.70. CI = exp(−0.35 ± 1.96 × 0.12) = exp(−0.35 ± 0.235) = exp(−0.585) to exp(−0.115) = 0.56 to 0.89. The group (or one-unit increase) has a 30% lower hazard of the event at any time during follow-up, among those still event-free, with the data compatible with an 11% to 44% lower hazard. It is not “30% lower risk”.

3. Explain why proportional hazards concerns the ratio of hazards between groups, not the hazard level itself.

Cox’s model is h(t) = h₀(t) × exp(bx). The baseline hazard h₀(t) may rise or fall freely over time (dropout climbing as a scheme ages); that is not a violation. What must stay constant is the multiplier exp(b), the ratio between the groups’ hazards at each moment, because the model estimates a single b for the whole follow-up.

1. A cohort study reports that TB patients who “ever received” a nutrition kit had 20 deaths in 1,000 person-months, against 30 deaths in 1,000 person-months in those who never did. Kits were given at the end of month 2, and 200 of the kit group’s person-months fell before the kit. Recompute the rates with kit receipt as a time-varying exposure, and the rate ratio before and after.

Naive: kit 20/1,000 = 2.0 per 100 person-months; no kit 30/1,000 = 3.0 per 100; rate ratio 2.0/3.0 = 0.67.

The 200 pre-kit person-months are immortal time: a patient had to survive to month 2 to receive the kit, so no deaths could fall in them. They are unexposed time. Corrected: kit 20 deaths in 1,000 − 200 = 800 person-months = 2.5 per 100; no kit 30 deaths in 1,000 + 200 = 1,200 person-months = 2.5 per 100; rate ratio 1.00. The apparent 33% reduction was entirely immortal-time bias.

2. In the CBHI cohort, you suspect the effect of distance changes over follow-up and you only need to adjust for it. Name a way to do this and what you give up.

Stratify on distance (for example, near vs far, split at the median): a stratified Cox model. Each stratum gets its own baseline hazard, so PH need not hold for distance. You give up an HR for distance, and a categorised distance adjusts less finely than the continuous variable (the intervention HR was 0.61 with a two-level stratum against 0.58 with continuous distance). Alternatively, keep distance in the model with a time-varying coefficient (a distance × time term), which does estimate how its effect changes.

1. Five patients: event of interest at week 1, competing event at week 2, event of interest at week 3, censored at week 4, event of interest at week 5. Compute the CIF of the event of interest at week 3, and 1 − KM at week 3 with the competing event censored.

CIF: week 1, 5 at risk, S(1₋) = 1: increment 1 × 1/5 = 0.200; S becomes 0.800. Week 2, competing event, 4 at risk: S = 0.800 × 3/4 = 0.600. Week 3, 3 at risk: increment 0.600 × 1/3 = 0.200. CIF(3) = 0.400.

1 − KM (competing event censored): week 1, 1 − 1/5 = 0.8; week 2, no step (censored); week 3, 3 at risk, × 2/3. KM = 0.8 × 2/3 = 0.533, so 1 − KM = 0.467. It overstates the probability of the event by 0.067, because it treats the patient with the competing event as though they could still have the event of interest.

2. A district study of elderly patients after hip fracture asks (a) whether diabetes raises the rate of re-fracture among those still alive, and (b) what proportion of patients will re-fracture within two years, for service planning. Death is common. Which model suits each question?

  1. An aetiological question about the rate among those still at risk: the cause-specific hazard model (a Cox model for re-fracture with deaths censored). (b) A question about the actual proportion who re-fracture in a population where many die first: the cumulative incidence function (Aalen–Johansen), and, with covariates, the Fine–Gray subdistribution hazard model. 1 − KM would overstate (b) because deaths are common.
